title: Hormonal coordination in humans
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank, except where marked for AQA GCSE Biology (8461) (status of the source: authored-gated-unreviewed). Terms and clues: 4.5.3-c22 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.5.3-c27 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.5.3-c06 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.5.3-c26 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition. Questions: 4.5.3-q01, 4.5.3-q04, 4.5.3-q02, 4.5.3-q05, 4.5.3-q03, 4.5.3-q06, 4.5.3-q07, 4.5.3-q08, 4.5.3-q09.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: secondary sex characteristics
items.clue: The features that develop during puberty, caused by reproductive hormones.

items.label: luteinising hormone (LH)
items.clue: A hormone involved in the menstrual cycle which stimulates the release of the egg.

items.label: pancreas
items.clue: The gland that monitors and controls blood glucose concentration by producing hormones.

items.label: follicle stimulating hormone (FSH)
items.clue: A hormone involved in the menstrual cycle which causes maturation of an egg in the ovary.

questions.stem: A gland of the endocrine system secretes a hormone. How does that hormone reach the organ where it produces an effect, and how do its effects compare with those of the nervous system?

options.text: carried along nerves; effects are slower but last longer
carried in the blood; effects are faster but end much sooner
carried along nerves; effects are faster but end sooner
carried in the blood; effects are slower but last longer

questions.explanation: Glands secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream and the blood carries the hormone to a target organ; compared to the nervous system the effects are slower but act for longer.

questions.stem: After a meal, the blood glucose concentration of a person who does not have diabetes rises above the normal level. What happens next?

options.text: insulin is released and glycogen forms in the blood
insulin is released and so glucose leaves the cells
insulin is released but the cells fail to respond
insulin is released and glucose enters the cells

questions.explanation: If the blood glucose concentration is too high, the pancreas produces the hormone insulin that causes glucose to move from the blood into the cells.

questions.stem: A student labels endocrine glands on a diagram of the human body. Which label has been placed in the correct position?

options.text: the adrenal gland labelled inside the brain
the thyroid gland labelled in the lower neck
the pituitary gland labelled below the stomach
the pancreas labelled at the base of the brain

questions.explanation: The thyroid is found in the neck, and students should be able to identify its position on a diagram of the human body.

questions.stem: A person's blood glucose concentration is too high. What happens to the excess glucose?

options.text: it is changed into glycogen in the blood
it is released from the cells into the blood
it is changed into glycogen in the pancreas
it moves into cells and is stored as glycogen

questions.explanation: Insulin causes glucose to move from the blood into the cells, and in liver and muscle cells excess glucose is converted to glycogen for storage.

questions.stem: Why is the pituitary gland described as a 'master gland'?

options.text: its hormones make other glands release hormones
its hormones produce all the body effects directly
its hormones travel to the glands along nerves
its hormones act on every organ in the body

questions.explanation: The pituitary gland secretes several hormones into the blood in response to body conditions, and these act on other glands to stimulate other hormones to be released.

options.text: the body cells no longer respond to insulin
the pancreas releases insulin when glucose is low
the pancreas fails to produce enough insulin
the pancreas is affected by a person's diet

questions.explanation: Type 1 diabetes is a disorder in which the pancreas fails to produce sufficient insulin, and it is characterised by uncontrolled high blood glucose levels.

questions.stem: A person with Type 2 diabetes has a normal concentration of insulin in the blood but a high blood glucose concentration. Why?

options.text: their pancreas has completely stopped making insulin
their insulin cannot act on glucose in the blood
their body cells no longer respond to insulin
their insulin is released when blood glucose is low

questions.explanation: In Type 2 diabetes the body cells no longer respond to insulin produced by the pancreas, so glucose is not moved from the blood into the cells even though insulin is present.

questions.stem: A graph shows blood glucose concentration for two hours after a glucose drink. For a person without diabetes the concentration rises to a peak and then returns to its starting level. For a person with untreated Type 1 diabetes it rises higher and stays high. What does the graph show about the person with Type 1 diabetes?

options.text: not enough insulin is produced to lower glucose
their body cells have stopped responding to insulin
their insulin cannot change glucose to glycogen
their insulin is produced when glucose is low

questions.explanation: The concentration stays high because the pancreas fails to produce sufficient insulin, so glucose is not moved from the blood into the cells and the level is not brought back down.

questions.stem: Several hours after a meal, the blood glucose concentration of a person falls below the normal level. Which change restores it?

options.text: insulin is released and stored glycogen changes to glucose
glucagon is released and glucose changes to glycogen
glucagon is released and glycogen changes to glucose
insulin is released and glucose changes to glycogen

questions.explanation: If the blood glucose concentration is too low, the pancreas produces glucagon, which causes glycogen to be converted into glucose and released into the blood.
